period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Before the Battle — Activating Prior Knowledge and Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Pair discussion on Republic Day Parade and bravery awards
Group discussion on qualities a soldier should have

phases.description: Teacher introduces the chapter by showing the title and asking students what they know about the Param Vir Chakra. Students share brief responses before settling into the lesson.
Reading for Comprehension — pre-reading pair discussion on Republic Day Parade highlights and bravery awards. Students share observations with the class in brief turns.
Reading for Comprehension — group discussion on soldier qualities and a personal message students would share with a soldier. Teacher facilitates and notes key words on the board.
Teacher reads aloud the opening two pages of the prose (p.49–52), students follow along. Teacher pauses to clarify key terms such as 'infiltrators' and 'Operation Gulmarg'.

periods.teacher_notes: This period sets the motivational frame for the chapter; the pre-reading discussions on bravery awards and soldier qualities prime students to engage personally with Major Sharma's story. Next period will continue shared reading and move into comprehension events. Students who have relatives in the armed forces may be invited to share briefly — handle with sensitivity.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Reading the Battle Narrative and Ordering Events

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Arrange key events of Major Sharma's life in chronological order

homework.task_brief: Read Extract 1 questions and draft personal responses

phases.description: Teacher reads aloud the central battle narrative (p.52–58) with students following; teacher pauses at Major Sharma's legendary last words to ask students what the words reveal about his character.
Reading for Comprehension — students work individually to arrange eight events in chronological order (Let us discuss, p.59). Pairs compare answers and resolve differences.
Class discussion to confirm the correct sequence; teacher links each event to the prose summary's timeline, reinforcing Sharma's progression from training to posthumous recognition.

periods.teacher_notes: The chronological ordering task helps students grasp the full arc from Major Sharma's 1923 birth to his posthumous PVC — ensure students distinguish the Arakan Campaign from the Battle of Badgam. Next period will focus on Extract-based inference questions. Extract 1 questions are assigned as homework preparation so students read the extract closely before class.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Inference and Reflection — Courage Under Devastating Fire

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Extract 1 — inference and assertion-reason questions
Extended reflection: last words, leadership, and legacy

phases.description: Teacher reviews homework responses on Extract 1 by cold-calling pairs; key misconceptions about the assertion-reason format are clarified on the board.

Reading for Comprehension — class works through Extract 1 (p.59–60): MCQ on battlefield conditions, assertion-reason on Sharma's fearlessness, and fill-in on what he did under fire. Teacher guides inference step by step.

Reading for Comprehension — teacher-led discussion on the extended reflection questions (p.61): Sharma's last words, why his leadership was critical, and how his values apply to daily life. Students respond orally in turns.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse Assertion-Reason format — model a think-aloud before releasing to pairs. The reflection on Sharma's last words ('I shall not withdraw an inch') is the emotional centrepiece of the prose; allow genuine student responses rather than rushing to a 'correct' answer. Extract 2 questions (p.60–61) are not covered in class; direct students to read them independently as self-study.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Listening to the PVC and Speaking for the Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen to PVC talk; fill blanks with exact words heard
Group speech on duty to the nation using sentence prompts

phases.description: Teacher briefly introduces the listening segment on the Param Vir Chakra, asking students to keep pens ready for note-taking and to listen for specific details.
Listening — teacher reads the PVC transcript (p.98) aloud twice; students complete five fill-in-the-blank sentences capturing exact words. Answers are discussed and verified with the class.
Transition: teacher connects the PVC's significance to the speaking task by asking, 'If Major Sharma sacrificed his life for the nation, what can we do as citizens today?'

Speaking — groups of four to five prepare and deliver a two-minute talk on how they propose to serve the nation, choosing one theme (environment, health, helping others, or righteous conduct) and using the sentence prompts on p.66–67.

periods.teacher_notes: For the listening task, read the transcript at a measured pace and pause naturally at clause boundaries — students at this stage benefit from two readings before completing blanks. During speaking, ensure quieter students in each group are given a speaking turn; the Box 2.6i guidance on individual differences applies here. Next period moves to writing.
materials: Sentence prompt cards or board display

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Writing a Formal Letter of Enquiry to a Memorial

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Draft formal letter of enquiry to memorial incharge

phases.description: Teacher explains the letter of enquiry format using the sample on p.67, pointing out key structural features: sender address, date, salutation, body paragraphs, and formal closing.
Teacher models the opening paragraph on the board using one of the four required points (available dates for visits). Students contribute suggested phrases, developing register awareness.

Writing — students independently draft the full letter (p.67–68) covering all four enquiry points: available dates, tour duration, entry fees, and guidelines for student groups. Teacher circulates and provides formative feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is informal register slipping into formal letters — remind students that 'I want to know' must become 'I would be grateful if you could provide information regarding.' Students who finish early may proofread and revise for tone and format. Next period begins Section A's vocabulary and grammar work.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Battlefield Idioms, Collective Nouns, and Subject-Verb Agreement

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Match battlefield idioms; complete sentences using expressions
Match collective nouns for armed forces; fill blanks

homework.task_brief: Subject-verb agreement: fill blanks and correct passage

phases.description: Vocabulary and Grammar — teacher introduces the four battlefield idioms (fight to the last man, foil the plan, deliver a blow, hold their ground) through context in the prose. Students match them to situations in Column 2 (p.62) in pairs.
Students complete sentences A–D using the idioms from Column 1 (p.62); teacher reviews answers whole-class, focusing on connotation and context.

Vocabulary and Grammar — teacher introduces the four collective nouns for armed forces (regiment, squadron, fleet, battalion). Students match Column 1 to meanings and fill four blank sentences (p.62–63). Answers reviewed together.

periods.teacher_notes: Idiom tasks often see students selecting by word similarity rather than meaning — encourage reading the full situation before matching. The collective noun fill-in is excellent for checking transfer: if a student writes 'a fleet of soldiers', comprehension of the term is incomplete. Tasks on over- prefix verbs (p.64) and noun-verb spelling pairs (p.64) are noted as self-study pointers for independent follow-up; subject-verb agreement sentences are assigned as homework.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Exploring Gallantry Awards and Women in the Armed Forces

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Research gallantry awards and women's roles in armed forces

phases.description: Teacher briefly introduces the twenty-one PVC awardees framework from p.68, highlighting Major Sharma as the first and Captain Vikram Batra as the last, providing context for the project.
Beyond-text — students read the passage on Captain Vikram Batra (p.68–69) and begin group research on the three gallantry awards (PVC, MVC, Vir Chakra), noting criteria and key recipients.

Groups share their initial findings in a brief oral round; teacher facilitates a focused discussion on the role of women in the Indian Armed Forces, drawing on students' prior knowledge before directing them to p.69 for more information.

periods.teacher_notes: This period closes Section A; the patriotic songs task from 'Let us explore' (p.69) is noted as a self-study pointer and may be shared informally at the start of the next session. The transition to Section B (the poem) should be framed as a tonal shift — from national heroism to everyday human compassion.
materials: Reference material on gallantry awards (if available)

periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem — Empathy at the Crossing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Pre-reading: associate words with elderly/student; meaning of 'ragged'
Arrange poem events in correct sequence

phases.description: Pre-reading (p.70): students recall a time they helped someone and write two feeling-words; pairs share briefly. Teacher builds empathy frame before introducing the poem.
Teacher reads the full poem aloud expressively (p.70–72); students follow in textbooks. Teacher pauses at 'somebody's mother' repetition and the boy's whispered offer to highlight tone shifts.

Reading for Comprehension — pre-reading word-association task: students circle words for elderly person, underline words for school student from the word list (p.70). Pairs share reasoning; teacher confirms the MCQ meaning of 'ragged'.
Reading for Comprehension — students individually arrange the eight poem events in correct sequence (p.73). Answers compared in pairs and verified whole-class.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's AABB couplet structure and ballad-like rhythm make it ideal for expressive teacher read-aloud — model the gentle, sympathetic tone rather than a dramatic one. The word-association task primes students to notice the contrast between the elderly woman's frailty and the boys' energy, which is the poem's central tension. Next period continues with poetic devices and imagery.

periods.activity_title: Poetic Devices, Imagery, and Vocabulary from the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Pick examples of simile, alliteration, repetition from poem
Explain why 'Somebody's Mother' is repeated; complete analogy
Match poem words to underlined phrases in Column 2

phases.description: Reading for Comprehension — students locate examples of simile ('like a flock of sheep'), alliteration ('firm and strong'), and repetition ('somebody's mother') in the poem (p.73). Teacher leads brief discussion on the effect of each device.

Reading for Comprehension — students complete the sentence explaining why the phrase 'somebody's mother' is repeated, and the analogy (old woman: vulnerable :: young boy: ___) from p.74. Pairs share; teacher draws out the poem's moral pivot.

Vocabulary and Grammar — students match poem words (hastened, heeded, stir, lend, piled, offered) to underlined phrases in Column 2 (p.76). Teacher reviews answers and elicits sentences using each word in a new context.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may confuse alliteration and repetition — clarify that alliteration is the same initial sound while repetition is the same word or phrase recurring. The analogy task is open-ended; accept 'compassionate and empowered' or similar. The imagery fill-in (p.73) and idiom matching for 'hand' (p.77) are left as self-study; next period covers listening and speaking for Section B.

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Young Hero and Speaking from Experience

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen again; complete five fill-in sentences with exact words
Pair narration of a helping incident using cue cards

phases.description: Teacher frames the listening segment by telling students they will hear a news broadcast about a young person whose act of courage mirrors the poem's values. Students prepare to listen actively.

Listening — teacher reads the transcript about Rohan Ramchandra Bahir (p.99) at natural pace. Students listen for the fill-in details on the first reading; second reading allows completion of all five blank sentences (p.78). Answers verified whole-class.
Brief discussion linking Rohan's real-life act to the poem's boy — teacher asks, 'What quality do Rohan and the 'gayest laddie' share?' Students respond in pairs then share with class.

Speaking — pairs narrate an incident where they helped someone, using one of the four cue cards (at school / at the market place / in the neighbourhood / in the playground) and sentence prompts from p.79. Each pair performs for another pair; teacher circulates offering brief formative feedback on fluency and detail.

periods.teacher_notes: The picture-sequencing task (p.78, task index 0) requires physical pictures from the textbook — if projection is unavailable, describe the six images verbally and ask students to number them; it is noted here as a sequencing alternative. The '-ed' pronunciation sort (p.79, speaking task index 0) is a useful warm-up that can be inserted before the narration if time allows. Next period moves to writing and beyond-text for Section B.

periods.activity_title: Diary Writing and Gratitude — Extending Empathy Beyond the Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Write diary entry about a day spent helping someone
Research motherland/fatherland countries; make gratitude card

phases.description: Teacher reads the diary entry format and opening prompt from p.80 aloud, discussing what makes a diary entry personal and reflective — tone, first person, honest emotion.

Writing — students draft their diary entry (p.80) covering: whom they helped, the situation, place and time, how they helped, the person's reaction, their own feelings, and why they would do it again. Teacher circulates providing formative feedback on voice and structure.
Teacher introduces the beyond-text activity (p.80–81): the Sanskrit verse from the Atharva Veda and the concept of 'motherland/fatherland'. Groups of four begin listing countries they know.

Beyond-text — groups compile their motherland/fatherland findings and begin designing a gratitude card for their mother or grandmother using the prompts on p.81. Groups share one or two findings with the class before the period ends.

periods.teacher_notes: The diary entry benefits from the emotional resonance students may still have from the poem — encourage them to draw on a real memory rather than an invented one for authenticity. The gratitude card project may extend beyond class into home; students should bring materials from home if recycled materials are not available at school. Section B is now complete; Section C begins next period.
materials: Recycled paper and art materials for gratitude card

periods.section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
periods.activity_title: Reading Kurien's Letter — Values, Integrity, and Language in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Identify facts and opinions in Kurien's letter
Replace underlined words with correct synonyms from the box

homework.task_brief: Read Extract 2 questions on grandmother's role; draft answers

phases.description: Teacher reads the opening two pages of Kurien's letter (p.82–84) aloud with students following; teacher pauses at the contrast between telephone calls and written letters to ask students which medium they prefer and why.

Reading for Comprehension — students individually classify eight statements as fact or opinion (p.85–86), then compare with a partner. Teacher leads whole-class review, focusing on statements 3 and 4 which are subtly evaluative.

Vocabulary and Grammar — students replace underlined words in six sentences with correct synonyms (essential, swift, lifelong, momentary, useful, splendid) from p.88. Teacher reviews answers, drawing attention to 'abiding' as a Kurien signature word linked to his life's work.

periods.teacher_notes: The fact-vs-opinion task is challenging because Kurien writes in first person and several statements blend personal conviction with reportable truth — model one example before releasing students. The remaining vocabulary and grammar tasks (expressions matching, em dash punctuation, contractions vs possessives, prepositional phrases) are rich but cannot fit this period; teachers should assign the expressions matching (p.89) as self-study and address punctuation and possessives informally during writing feedback.

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student analyses a narrative prose text for chronological structure and character-driven inference using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Major Sharma's battle at Badgam, last words, leadership, posthumous PVC award.
items.item_stem:
When the enemy attacked D Company at Badgam on 3 November 1947, Major Somnath Sharma took several actions under devastating fire. Read the four statements below and identify which TWO are true based on the account of the Battle of Badgam.

1. Major Sharma identified the initial enemy attack as a decoy and called for air strikes.
2. Major Sharma ordered an immediate withdrawal when the enemy came within 50 yards.
3. Major Sharma filled ammunition magazines for his gunners while moving under enemy fire.
4. Major Sharma surrendered D Company's position after losing half his men.

Write the numbers of the two TRUE statements and provide one piece of evidence from the passage to support each.

options.text: Major Sharma identified the initial enemy attack as a decoy and called for air strikes.
Major Sharma ordered an immediate withdrawal when the enemy came within 50 yards.
Major Sharma filled ammunition magazines for his gunners while moving under enemy fire.
Major Sharma surrendered D Company's position after losing half his men.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 1 is supported by the narrative's account that Sharma correctly identified an initial attack as a decoy and called for air strikes; Statement 3 is supported by the description of him filling ammunition magazines for his gunners under fire. Statement 2 is false because Sharma explicitly refused to withdraw, declaring he would fight to the last man; Statement 4 is false because his men held the position for six more hours after his death rather than surrendering.

2. Major Sharma ordered an immediate withdrawal when the enemy came within 50 yards.
3. Major Sharma filled ammunition magazines for his gunners while moving under enemy fire.
4. Major Sharma surrendered D Company's position after losing half his men.

Write the numbers of the two TRUE statements and provide one piece of evidence from the passage to support each.

items.source_lo: Student identifies poetic devices and interprets theme and tone using a narrative poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Frail elderly woman at a snowy crossing; one compassionate schoolboy; AABB couplets; 'somebody's mother' repetition.
items.item_stem:
Read the following stanza from the poem 'Somebody's Mother' by Mary Dow Brine:

'She's somebody's mother, boys, you know,
For all she's aged and poor and slow,
And I hope some fellow will lend a hand
To help my mother, you understand,
If ever she's poor and old and grey,
When her own dear boy is far away.'

(a) What poetic device is used in the repetition of 'somebody's mother' throughout the poem, and what effect does it create on the reader?
(b) The poem follows an AABB rhyme scheme. Identify one rhyming pair from the stanza above and explain how the rhyme scheme contributes to the poem's ballad-like quality.

expected_elements: Identifies repetition as the device and links it to the poem's moral pivot of shared humanity.
Explains that the repetition shifts the reader from pity to empathy by universalising the woman's identity.
Names a correct rhyming pair from the stanza, e.g., 'know/slow' or 'hand/understand' or 'grey/away'.
Connects the regular AABB rhythm to a gentle, story-telling ballad quality that suits the sympathetic tone.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student distinguishes fact from opinion and draws inferences from an autobiographical informational text using letter format as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Kurien's letter to grandson Siddharth; integrity, cooperative choice in Anand, Padma Vibhushan ceremony.
items.item_stem:
In his letter to his grandson Siddharth, Dr. Verghese Kurien writes: 'To be quite honest, service to our nation's farmers was not the career I had envisioned for myself.' He also states that he received the Padma Vibhushan in 1999 and that Siddharth placed the medal around his neck during the ceremony.

Read the three statements below. Label each as FACT or OPINION and give a reason for your classification.

1. Dr. Kurien received the Padma Vibhushan award in 1999.
2. Service to the nation's farmers was the most meaningful career choice anyone could make.
3. Dr. Kurien chose to work at a small dairy cooperative in Anand, Gujarat.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is a FACT because the letter explicitly names the Padma Vibhushan ceremony in 1999 as a verifiable event. Statement 2 is an OPINION because it is a value judgement about career choice, not a verifiable claim. Statement 3 is a FACT because Kurien's letter directly states that he made the choice to work at the cooperative in Anand, Gujarat, which is a reportable event.

1. The Param Vir Chakra is made of ________ metal.
2. At the centre of the medal, on a raised circle, is the ________.

items.source_context: Rohan Ramchandra Bahir saving a woman from Domri River; Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar 2023.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the special news broadcast about Rohan Ramchandra Bahir. After listening, complete the following sentences with one to three words from the broadcast.

1. Rohan was a ________-year-old student from Rajouri when he performed his act of bravery.
2. The woman had fallen into the ________ River while washing clothes.
3. Onlookers described Rohan as showing great ________ and courage despite the dangerous river conditions.
4. Rohan was honoured with the Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar 2023 by the President of India at ________.
items.question_text:
Listen to the special news broadcast about Rohan Ramchandra Bahir. After listening, complete the following sentences with one to three words from the broadcast.

1. Rohan was a ________-year-old student from Rajouri when he performed his act of bravery.
2. The woman had fallen into the ________ River while washing clothes.
3. Onlookers described Rohan as showing great ________ and courage despite the dangerous river conditions.
4. Rohan was honoured with the Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar 2023 by the President of India at ________.

items.source_lo: Student organises and delivers a structured group speech on a civic theme using public speaking conventions as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Citizens' duty to the nation; themes of environment, health, helping others, righteous conduct.
items.item_stem: Major Somnath Sharma believed that every citizen has a duty to serve the nation. In a group of four to five students, prepare and deliver a two-minute talk on how young citizens like you can contribute to the country. Choose ONE of the following themes: saving the environment, promoting health and well-being, helping others in the community, or practising righteous conduct. Your talk should have a clear opening, at least two specific examples of what you propose to do, and a closing statement that reflects your commitment.

expected_elements: Talk has a clear opening that introduces the chosen theme and the group's stance.
At least two specific, realistic examples of citizen action are described.
Language is formal and appropriate for a public-speaking context.
Closing statement reflects personal or collective commitment to the theme.
Each group member contributes at least one turn of speaking.

items.source_lo: Student narrates a personal experience with fluency and detail using guided pair conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Narrating an incident of helping someone; settings from daily life in school, market, neighbourhood, or playground.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the 'gayest laddie' pauses to help an elderly woman cross a slippery street — a small act that leaves a lasting impression on both of them. With a partner, take turns to narrate a real or imagined incident in which you helped someone in one of these settings: at school, at the marketplace, in the neighbourhood, or in the playground. When you speak, include: where and when it happened, who needed help and why, what you did, and how both of you felt afterwards.

expected_elements: Narration clearly identifies the setting and the person who needed help.
The sequence of events is logical: situation, action taken, outcome.
Speaker describes feelings of both parties, showing empathy.
Language is natural and spoken in complete sentences without excessive hesitation.

items.item_stem: Your school is planning a trip to a war memorial in your state to honour the memory of soldiers who gave their lives for the nation — much like Major Somnath Sharma, India's first Param Vir Chakra recipient. Write a formal letter of enquiry to the In-charge of the memorial. In your letter, request information about: (a) dates available for school group visits, (b) the expected duration of the tour, (c) any entry fees applicable for students, and (d) specific guidelines your school group must follow during the visit. Use a proper formal letter format with sender address, date, salutation, body paragraphs, and a formal closing.

expected_elements: Letter follows full formal format: address, date, salutation, body, closing.
All four enquiry points addressed clearly in the body paragraphs.
Register is consistently formal throughout; no colloquial phrasing.
Sentences are grammatically accurate and logically organised.
Closing includes a polite request for a timely reply.

items.source_lo: Student writes a reflective personal diary entry using first-person voice, emotional honesty, and sequential narration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A day spent helping someone; including feelings, reaction of the person helped, and personal reflection.
items.item_stem: The boy in 'Somebody's Mother' helps an elderly woman cross a dangerous street and returns to his friends with his 'young heart happy and well content.' Think about a day when you helped someone — a classmate, a neighbour, a family member, or a stranger. Write a diary entry for that day. In your entry, describe: who you helped and what the situation was, what you did and where it happened, how the person reacted, how you felt during and after helping, and why you would choose to do it again. You may begin your entry: 'Dear Diary, Today I feel was a special day…'

expected_elements: Entry is written in first person with a diary heading (date and time).
Situation, action, and person's reaction are described in sequence.
Writer's feelings during and after the incident are expressed honestly.
Entry includes a personal reflection on why the act mattered.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student writes a personal letter expressing gratitude and articulating values inspired by a mentor using informal letter format as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Letter to grandparents; lessons inherited, values shaped, inspiration to contribute to society.
items.item_stem: Dr. Verghese Kurien wrote a letter to his grandson Siddharth to pass on the values he had learned — integrity, humility, hard work, and commitment to the common good. He believed that the lessons from those closest to us shape who we become. Write a personal letter to your grandparents (or an elder who has guided you) thanking them for the lessons they have taught you. In your letter, mention: one specific thing they taught you and how it changed your thinking or behaviour, one story or example from their life that continues to inspire you, and how their values encourage you to contribute to your community or country.

expected_elements: Letter uses personal letter format with greeting, body paragraphs, and warm closing.
One specific lesson is named with a concrete example of how it influenced the writer.
An inspiring story or action from the elder's life is described in some detail.
Writer articulates a genuine intention to contribute to community or society.
Tone is warm, respectful, and personal throughout.

items.item_stem: The prose about Major Somnath Sharma uses several expressions and collective nouns drawn from military language. Match each expression in Column A with its most accurate meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A|Column B
hold their ground|(i) to persist and resist without retreating
foil the plan|(ii) to prevent an opponent's scheme from succeeding
deliver a blow|(iii) to cause significant harm or damage to an opponent
flight of aircraft / squadron|(iv) a small unit of twelve to twenty-four aircraft and their crews

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: hold their ground — (i); foil the plan — (ii); deliver a blow — (iii); flight of aircraft / squadron — (iv).

items.item_stem:
Dr. Verghese Kurien's letter to his grandson is full of precise word choices that capture his values and experiences. Read each sentence below, which is inspired by themes from the letter. Choose the word from the box that best replaces the underlined word without changing the meaning of the sentence.

Word box: essential, swift, lifelong, momentary, splendid

1. The joy of hearing good news on the telephone is brief and soon fades away.
2. Integrity was a permanent value that guided Dr. Kurien throughout his career.
3. The award ceremony in 1999 was a magnificent occasion that Siddharth would never forget.
4. Collaboration with others is a necessary part of achieving any great goal.
5. The messenger carried the news across the village in a quick and efficient manner.

items.source_lo: Student researches and presents findings on India's gallantry awards and women's roles in the armed forces using project work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Twenty-one PVC awardees; Captain Vikram Batra; Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra; women in Indian Armed Forces.
items.item_stem:
The prose tells us that twenty-one soldiers have received the Param Vir Chakra — from Major Somnath Sharma, the first, to Captain Vikram Batra, the last. India also has two other gallantry awards: the Maha Vir Chakra and the Vir Chakra. Working in a group of four, prepare a short presentation (or a poster) that covers the following:

(a) The criteria for awarding the Param Vir Chakra, the Maha Vir Chakra, and the Vir Chakra — what distinguishes one from another.
(b) The name and a brief account of ONE Param Vir Chakra awardee other than Major Somnath Sharma.
(c) TWO roles that women currently hold in the Indian Armed Forces.

Share your findings with the class.

expected_elements: Criteria for all three gallantry awards are correctly distinguished and explained.
One PVC awardee other than Sharma is named with an accurate brief account of their action.
Two specific roles of women in the Indian Armed Forces are identified with brief descriptions.
Presentation or poster is organised, legible, and shared clearly with the class.

items.source_lo: Student investigates cultural concepts of motherland and fatherland and creates a gratitude artefact using interdisciplinary project work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Countries referring to homeland as motherland or fatherland; Atharva Veda verse; gratitude card for mother or grandmother.
items.item_stem:
The poem 'Somebody's Mother' celebrates the bond between a mother and her child, and India's ancient Atharva Veda declares 'माता भूमि: पुत्रोऽहं पृथिव्या:' — meaning 'Earth is my mother and I am her child.' Many nations refer to their homeland as 'motherland' while others say 'fatherland.'

Complete the following two tasks:

(a) Working in a group of four, find the names of at least THREE countries that refer to their nation as 'motherland' and at least TWO countries that call their nation 'fatherland'. Prepare a brief note explaining why you think different cultures may use different terms.

(b) Individually, create a gratitude card for your mother or grandmother using recycled or available materials. On the card, write at least five things you are grateful to her for, and mention two things you will do regularly to support or help her.

expected_elements: At least three 'motherland' countries and two 'fatherland' countries correctly identified.
Brief cultural explanation is thoughtful and goes beyond a simple list.
Gratitude card names five specific, genuine things the student appreciates.
Two practical commitments to help the family member are stated clearly.
